title: Read and repair a weave plan
subtitle: Trace the same crossing from front to back.
summary: Explore a six-by-six plain-weave plan, introduce a structural error and repair one complete weft sequence. Use the accompanying packet to prepare a real paper demonstration.
audience: Beginners; no notation or craft experience required.
scope: This is a digital structural draft and physical-session preparation. A real specimen, photographs and independent reproduction are still missing. It is not a demonstrated physical lesson.

passages.title: A structure does not determine every material property
passages.text: In plain weave, the weft alternates over and under individual warp threads. The appearance of a textile also depends on the material and the properties of its threads.
passages.context: Original paraphrase of the technical description. It supports the generic interlacing idea, not this paper procedure, a unique cultural origin or a claim to represent all Greek textile practice.

claims.text: The specified checkerboard plan alternates at adjacent crossings in both directions.
claims.qualification: An ideal binary model with equally spaced strips; not a measurement of a real specimen.

claims.text: Correct symbolic alternation does not establish physical handling skill or fabric properties.
claims.qualification: Tension, packing, drape, continuous yarn and finished edges are outside this model.

context: In this diagram, warp strips W1–W6 form columns and weft strips F1–F6 form rows. These chosen axes are not a universal orientation for every woven object.
Front convention: the weft is above the warp when the row and column numbers sum to an even number. The bit string stores that front relation only.
Back view means turning the specimen over about a vertical axis: top stays top, warp labels reverse order, and the visible top strip at every crossing changes. It is not a rotation within the plane.
A six-column checkerboard may look the same after reversing columns and swapping visible strips. Trace the labels to establish that the view changed.

The error control changes a symbolic crossing only. It can produce a run of three repeated crossings in an interior row. The repair control models withdrawing and reweaving the whole selected weft strip.
A real repair requires accessible, unsealed ends and support for neighboring strips. Those strips may move; physical feasibility and instruction clarity have not been observed.

steps.title: 0 · Lay out the warp plan
steps.text: Plan six pre-cut warp strips with labels W1–W6 and a front/top marker. Keep their ends accessible. A practitioner must first verify the real materials and temporary support.

steps.title: 1 · First weft
steps.text: Plan F1 across W1–W6 as over, under, over, under, over, under when viewed from the front. The diagram is a schematic, not a photograph.

steps.title: 2 · Reverse the phase
steps.text: Plan F2 as under, over, under, over, under, over. Adjacent rows now alternate at the same warp crossing.

steps.title: 3 · Continue the first phase
steps.text: Plan F3 with the same front sequence as F1. Check canonical labels before comparing the opposite side.

steps.title: 4 · Continue the second phase
steps.text: Plan F4 with the same front sequence as F2. In a real sample, record any displacement or assistance rather than assuming the diagram proves stability.

steps.title: 5 · Add the fifth weft
steps.text: Plan F5 like F1. Keep the real strip ends unsealed if a later whole-strip repair is to be demonstrated.

steps.title: 6 · Inspect both sides and plan a repair
steps.text: Plan F6 like F2. For a real demonstration, photograph the labelled front, turn about the vertical axis and photograph the back. A proposed repair withdraws the entire chosen weft, supports its neighbors and reweaves the required sequence. This still needs physical verification.

activity.transfer: On a new labelled four-by-four plan, explain which physical crossing a back-view cell represents. Then list what evidence a real paper sample would add that the grid cannot supply.
rubric: Name canonical warp/weft IDs and the declared flip axis.
Separate front-relative data from the top strip visible on the chosen side.
Describe the actual repeated crossings and a whole-strip repair, not an impossible isolated physical crossing change.
Distinguish symbolic consistency, physical completion and observed handling.
State which photographs, material details and independent observations remain missing.
